title: Generative Classifiers: Gaussian Discriminant Analysis and Naive Bayes
description: Classification by modeling how each class generates its inputs and applying Bayes' rule.
overview: Logistic regression models P(y | x) directly. A generative classifier takes the opposite route. It models how the inputs look within each class, P(x | y), and the prior P(y), and then uses Bayes' rule to obtain P(y | x). The extra modeling work pays off in two ways: when the assumptions are close to true the classifier needs less data, and the model can generate new examples and handle missing inputs.
We study the two classic cases: Gaussian discriminant analysis for continuous features and naive Bayes for discrete features such as words.
objectives: Contrast generative and discriminative classifiers and apply Bayes' rule to classify.
Fit a Gaussian discriminant analysis model, derive its decision boundary, and show its relation to logistic regression.
Distinguish LDA from QDA and count their parameters.
Build a naive Bayes classifier, apply Laplace smoothing, and compute predictions in log space.
Explain when generative models beat discriminative ones and when they lose.

sections.title: Generative versus discriminative models
body: Suppose you want to tell cats from dogs in photos. One approach is to learn what separates them directly: "photos with this ear shape and snout length are dogs." Another is to learn what a typical cat photo looks like, and what a typical dog photo looks like, and then label a new photo by asking which description it matches better. The first approach is discriminative and the second is generative.

A **discriminative** model learns P(y | x) or a decision rule directly. Logistic regression and support vector machines are discriminative. A **generative** model learns the joint distribution through two pieces, the **class prior** P(y) and the class-conditional density P(x | y). Bayes' rule then gives the **posterior**:

body.eq: P(y | x) = P(x | y) P(y) / P(x),    P(x) = Σ_y P(x | y) P(y)

body: Bayes' rule just reverses the direction of a conditional probability. Example: 1% of emails are spam (the prior). If an email is spam, the word "prize" appears in 40% of cases, and if it is not spam, in 2%. For an email containing "prize", spam contributes 0.01 × 0.40 = 0.004 and non-spam contributes 0.99 × 0.02 = 0.0198, so P(spam | prize) = 0.004/(0.004 + 0.0198) = 0.17. The word is strong evidence (20 times more likely under spam), but the low prior keeps the posterior modest. The prior and the evidence are both needed.
For classification the denominator is the same for all classes and can be ignored:

If the true P(y | x) were known, predicting its argmax would minimize the error rate. This is the **Bayes optimal classifier**, and its error is the **Bayes error**, the floor that no classifier can beat. Every method tries to approximate it.

list: Generative models make stronger assumptions about the form of P(x | y). If they are right, estimates are accurate with little data. If they are wrong, the model is biased.
Discriminative models spend their capacity only on the boundary between classes. They make fewer assumptions and are usually more accurate with plenty of data.
Generative models can sample new inputs, deal naturally with missing features (marginalize them out) and use unlabeled data.

sections.title: Gaussian discriminant analysis
body: Picture the data as two clouds of points, one per class, each shaped like a blob that is dense in the middle and thins out toward the edges. GDA describes each blob by its center (the mean) and its shape (the covariance), then classifies a new point by asking which blob it more plausibly came from. In one dimension, with equal priors and equal spreads, this reduces to a simple rule: choose the class whose mean is closer.
For continuous x ∈ ℝⁿ, **Gaussian discriminant analysis** (GDA) assumes each class has a multivariate normal density (see the Gaussian in Multivariate Probability), with a shared covariance Σ:
The parameters (φ, μ₀, μ₁, Σ) are fit by maximizing the joint log-likelihood Σ ln p(x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}). The solution is closed-form and intuitive:
The prior is the class frequency, each mean is the class average, and the covariance is the pooled scatter around the class means.
Take the log of the ratio of the posteriors. The terms quadratic in x cancel because Σ is shared, leaving

eq: ln P(y = 1 | x)/P(y = 0 | x) = wᵀx + b
w = Σ⁻¹(μ₁ − μ₀),    b = −½(μ₁ᵀΣ⁻¹μ₁ − μ₀ᵀΣ⁻¹μ₀) + ln(φ/(1 − φ))

body: So the posterior has exactly the logistic form P(y = 1 | x) = σ(wᵀx + b). GDA and logistic regression produce the same type of classifier but estimate w and b differently: GDA through the class densities, logistic regression by maximizing the conditional likelihood directly.

example.title: One-dimensional GDA
example.problem: Class 0 has x = 1, 2, 3 and class 1 has x = 5, 6, 7. Fit GDA and find the posterior at x = 3, 4 and 5.
solution: φ = 0.5, μ₀ = 2, μ₁ = 6. The pooled variance is σ² = (1 + 0 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 1)/6 = 2/3.
The log-odds are 6x − 24: −6 at x = 3, 0 at x = 4, and 6 at x = 5. The posteriors are σ(−6) = 0.0025, 0.5 and σ(6) = 0.9975. The boundary x = 4 is the midpoint of the class means.

list: With a shared covariance the method is called **linear discriminant analysis** (LDA). The prior shifts the boundary toward the rarer class's mean by (σ²/(μ₁ − μ₀)) ln(φ₀/φ₁) in one dimension.

Letting each class have its own covariance Σ_k gives **quadratic discriminant analysis** (QDA), whose boundary is a quadric surface (a parabola, ellipse or hyperbola in two dimensions). It is more flexible and has more parameters, n(n + 1)/2 per class.
For K classes, use K means, one shared Σ and K priors. Predict the class with the largest linear discriminant δ_k(x) = xᵀΣ⁻¹μ_k − ½μ_kᵀΣ⁻¹μ_k + ln φ_k.
When n is large relative to m, the estimate of Σ is unreliable. Shrink it toward a diagonal matrix (regularized discriminant analysis).

sections.title: GDA or logistic regression?
body: If x | y is Gaussian with shared covariance, the posterior is logistic. The reverse does not hold: the logistic form arises from many other families, including Poisson distributions and other exponential families with shared structure.

Only that log-odds are linear in x
Better if the Gaussian assumption holds
Sensitive to outliers and non-Gaussian features
table.caption: Comparing the two classifiers.

body: Ng and Jordan (2002) showed that the generative model approaches its (higher) asymptotic error faster, using fewer examples, while the discriminative model reaches a lower error eventually. With little data the generative model often wins. With a lot of data and a messy distribution, logistic regression wins.

body.tip: When you are unsure, fit both and compare on held-out data. The logistic model is the safer default for a large data set.

sections.title: Naive Bayes
body: For discrete features such as the words in an email, modeling P(x | y) in full is hopeless. With n binary features there are 2ⁿ − 1 free probabilities per class. **Naive Bayes** makes one strong assumption: the features are **conditionally independent given the class**,
This cuts the parameters to n per class (for binary features). The classifier is

body.eq: ŷ = argmax_y  P(y) Π_j P(x_j | y)

body: Represent a document by binary indicators x_j = 1 if word j appears. The parameters are φ_{j|y} = P(x_j = 1 | y) and the prior φ_y. Maximum likelihood gives counting estimates,

eq: φ_{j|y} = (number of class-y documents containing word j) / (number of class-y documents)

body: If a word never occurred in the spam training emails, its estimated probability is 0, and any new email containing it receives probability 0 for the spam class, no matter how much other evidence there is. **Laplace smoothing** adds one imaginary occurrence and one imaginary non-occurrence of every word to every class:
It is the MAP estimate under a uniform prior on each probability, and it prevents zero probabilities.

example.title: A tiny spam filter
example.problem: The training emails are, as sets of words from the vocabulary {buy, now, meeting}: spam: {buy, now}, {buy}; ham: {now, meeting}, {meeting}. Classify the new email {buy, now} with Laplace smoothing.
solution: The priors are 0.5 and 0.5. Without smoothing, P(meeting | spam) = 0 and P(buy | ham) = 0, so an email such as {buy, meeting} would receive probability 0 for both classes. With smoothing, divide (count + 1) by (2 + 2):
For the email {buy, now}, meeting is absent, so we multiply by 1 − P(meeting | y):

body.h: Multinomial event model and log space

body: A model that counts word occurrences treats a document as a sequence of words drawn independently from a class-specific distribution over the vocabulary V. The estimate with Laplace smoothing is P(w | y) = (count of w in class y + 1)/(total tokens in class y + |V|). For spam tokens {buy ×2, now ×1} over three words this gives (0.5, 1/3, 1/6) for (buy, now, meeting), which sum to 1.

body.warn: Products of hundreds of small probabilities underflow to zero. Always compute in log space, ŷ = argmax [ ln P(y) + Σ_j ln P(x_j | y) ].

body.h: Why such a naive model works

body: The independence assumption is almost never true (the words 'new' and 'york' co-occur). Naive Bayes can still classify well, because classification needs only the correct ranking of the classes, not accurate probabilities. The probabilities it produces are often overconfident. It trains in one pass through the data, scales to huge vocabularies, and is a strong baseline for text. It is an example of high bias and low variance.

quiz.q: 5% of emails are spam. A certain word appears in 60% of spam and 3% of non-spam. For an email containing the word, P(spam) is about
quiz.why: Spam contributes 0.05 × 0.60 = 0.030 and non-spam 0.95 × 0.03 = 0.0285, so P = 0.030/0.0585 ≈ 0.51. The value 0.95 comes from using the likelihood ratio of 20 and ignoring the prior.

quiz.q: Which ability is a real advantage of a generative classifier over a discriminative one?
quiz.a: It can marginalize out missing features and sample new inputs
wrong: It makes fewer assumptions about the shape of the data
It is usually more accurate when there is a great deal of data
It spends all its capacity on the boundary between classes
quiz.why: Having a model of P(x | y) allows integrating out unobserved features and generating examples. The other options describe discriminative models.

quiz.q: The Bayes error of a problem is
quiz.a: the lowest error any classifier can reach, given the true P(y | x)
wrong: the error a naive Bayes classifier makes on its own training set
the extra error caused by wrongly assuming conditional independence
the training error of the best generative model for the problem
quiz.why: Predicting the argmax of the true posterior minimizes the error rate, and what remains is the floor that every method tries to approach.

quiz.q: Two classes have P(y = 0) = 0.9 and P(y = 1) = 0.1. For an input x, P(x | y = 0) = 0.02 and P(x | y = 1) = 0.10. The Bayes rule prediction is
wrong: class 1, since its likelihood 0.10 is larger
class 1, since the likelihood ratio of 5 always decides the class
neither: the scores tie
quiz.why: Compare P(x | y)P(y): 0.018 against 0.010. The likelihood favors class 1, but the prior is strong enough to reverse the decision.

quiz.q: 1D data: class 0 has x = 0, 2 and class 1 has x = 6, 8, 10. The pooled variance of the GDA model, using the maximum likelihood estimate, is
quiz.why: The means are 1 and 8. Squared deviations: 1 + 1 for class 0 and 4 + 0 + 4 for class 1, total 10, divided by m = 5 gives 2. Dividing by m − 1 would give 2.5.

quiz.q: For the same data (class 0: x = 0, 2; class 1: x = 6, 8, 10), the means are 1 and 8, so the midpoint is 4.5. The fitted GDA boundary is
quiz.a: about 4.38, shifted toward the rarer class 0
wrong: about 4.62, shifted toward the more common class 1
exactly 4.5, since priors do not affect the boundary
at 1, the mean of class 0
quiz.why: The class priors are 0.4 and 0.6, so the boundary shifts away from the more common class's mean, by (σ²/(μ₁ − μ₀)) ln(φ₀/φ₁) = (2/7)(−0.405) ≈ −0.12. The more common class gets the larger region.

quiz.q: Why is the GDA decision boundary linear when both classes share one covariance matrix Σ?
quiz.a: The quadratic terms are identical for both classes and cancel
wrong: The class priors are always equal, so the log-odds reduce to a straight line
Gaussian densities are symmetric about their means, which makes the boundary flat
The two classes then have the same mean, so the posteriors differ only in the prior
quiz.why: The quadratic term xᵀΣ⁻¹x appears in both class log-densities, so it drops out of the difference. With separate covariances it remains, giving a quadratic boundary.

quiz.q: Which statement about GDA and logistic regression is correct?
quiz.a: A logistic posterior can arise from non-Gaussian class densities, so it does not imply Gaussian classes
wrong: A logistic posterior implies that each class density is Gaussian
Logistic regression assumes the classes share a covariance matrix
GDA gives a softmax posterior, which is never logistic for two classes
quiz.why: Gaussian classes with shared covariance imply a logistic posterior, but the converse fails. This is why logistic regression, which assumes less, is more robust.

quiz.q: A problem has n = 4 features and K = 3 classes. How many covariance parameters do LDA and QDA estimate?
wrong: LDA 16, QDA 48
LDA 4, QDA 12
LDA 10, QDA 20
quiz.why: A symmetric 4×4 covariance has n(n + 1)/2 = 10 free entries. LDA uses one shared matrix, and QDA uses one for each of the 3 classes.

quiz.q: A GDA model has many features relative to the number of training examples, and the estimate of Σ is unreliable. A standard remedy is to
quiz.a: shrink the covariance estimate toward a diagonal matrix
wrong: switch to QDA so each class gets its own covariance
drop the class priors from the model
estimate the means by the overall average of all examples
quiz.why: Shrinkage (regularized discriminant analysis) stabilizes Σ. QDA would require estimating even more parameters, which makes the problem worse.

quiz.q: There are only 40 labeled examples and the features are roughly Gaussian within each class. Which method is likely to do better?
quiz.a: GDA, which reaches its asymptotic error with fewer examples
wrong: Logistic regression, since it always needs fewer examples
Neither, since a generative model needs more examples than parameters
Logistic regression, since it makes stronger assumptions
quiz.why: When its assumptions hold, the generative model gets accurate estimates quickly. Logistic regression is better eventually, with plenty of data.

quiz.q: A full joint distribution over 10 binary features needs how many free probabilities per class, and how many does naive Bayes need?
wrong: 1024 versus 10
100 versus 10
1023 versus 20
quiz.why: The full joint over 10 binary variables has 2¹⁰ − 1 = 1023 free entries. Conditional independence reduces this to one probability per feature, 10.

quiz.q: The naive Bayes assumption is that the features are
quiz.a: independent of one another once the class is known
wrong: independent of the class label, so the class carries no information
unconditionally independent of one another, whatever the class
Gaussian within each class, with a common variance
quiz.why: It is conditional independence given y. Unconditionally the features may be strongly dependent through the class.

quiz.q: In a Bernoulli naive Bayes spam filter, 8 spam emails were seen and the word "free" appeared in 5. With Laplace smoothing, P(free | spam) is
quiz.why: Add one imaginary occurrence and one non-occurrence: (5 + 1)/(8 + 2) = 0.6. The unsmoothed estimate is 5/8 = 0.625.

quiz.q: A multinomial model has a vocabulary of 4 words. Ham emails contain 20 tokens in total and "meeting" appears 3 times. With Laplace smoothing, P(meeting | ham) is
quiz.why: The estimate is (3 + 1)/(20 + 4) = 4/24 = 1/6. The denominator adds the vocabulary size, since every word receives one pseudo-count.

quiz.q: Why is a naive Bayes classifier computed in log space?
quiz.a: Long products underflow, while sums of logs are stable with the same argmax
wrong: Taking logs makes the features conditionally independent of one another
Logs turn the raw scores into calibrated probabilities for each class
Logs make Laplace smoothing unnecessary for words not seen in training
quiz.why: The logarithm is increasing, so the highest-scoring class is unchanged, and the sum of hundreds of log probabilities does not vanish the way a product does.

quiz.q: Naive Bayes often classifies text well even though word independence is clearly false. The best explanation is that
quiz.a: only the ranking of class scores matters, not accurate probabilities
wrong: the independence errors cancel exactly in the ratio of the posteriors
Laplace smoothing restores independence among the words in a document
its probabilities are well calibrated even when the assumption fails badly
quiz.why: The ranking of classes can survive badly distorted probabilities, which are in fact often overconfident. Naive Bayes is a high-bias, low-variance model.

summary: Generative classifiers model P(x | y) and P(y), then classify with Bayes' rule: ŷ = argmax P(x | y)P(y). Discriminative models fit P(y | x) directly.

GDA assumes Gaussian classes. The maximum likelihood fit uses the class frequencies, class means and pooled covariance. With a shared covariance the posterior is logistic and the boundary is linear (LDA); separate covariances give a quadratic boundary (QDA).
Generative models are more data-efficient when their assumptions hold. Logistic regression is more robust and wins with large data.
Naive Bayes assumes the features are conditionally independent given the class, which collapses the parameter count. Use Laplace smoothing and log probabilities.
Naive Bayes ranks classes well even when the independence assumption is false, but its probabilities are poorly calibrated.

problems.q: In the 1D GDA example (means 2 and 6, variance 2/3) the class priors are φ₁ = 0.2 and φ₀ = 0.8. Find the decision boundary.
problems.solution: The log-odds are 6x − 24 + ln(0.2/0.8) = 6x − 24 − 1.386. Setting it to zero gives x = 25.386/6 = 4.231.
problems.a: x ≈ 4.23: the boundary moves toward the rarer class mean.

problems.q: Class 1 data are (2, 3), (4, 3) and class 0 data are (1, 0), (3, 0). Compute φ, μ₀, μ₁ and the pooled covariance of the GDA model.
problems.a: φ = 0.5, μ₀ = (2, 0), μ₁ = (3, 3), Σ = [[1, 0], [0, 0]] (singular, since both classes have no spread in the second coordinate).

problems.q: A vocabulary has 5 words. Spam tokens total 40 and the word 'free' occurs 6 times in them. What is P('free' | spam) under the multinomial model with Laplace smoothing?
For a binary-feature naive Bayes classifier, P(spam) = 0.3 and a document has features whose likelihood ratio product is 40 in favor of spam (P(x | spam)/P(x | ham) = 40). Find P(spam | x).
problems.solution: Posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio = (0.3/0.7) × 40 = 17.14. Then P = 17.14/(1 + 17.14) = 0.945.

problems.q: Naive Bayes with n = 20 binary features and K = 3 classes: how many parameters are estimated?
problems.solution: Each class has 20 conditional probabilities, giving 60. The priors contribute K − 1 = 2 free parameters. Total 62.
